passage: Sofia had got a B-plus in chemistry, the best grade she'd ever had at her school in Madrid. She was proud for exactly ten minutes, until Layla, at the next desk, got an A-minus. Layla always seemed one step ahead: slightly better grades, slightly newer trainers, a family that went to the coast every August while Sofia's family went to her grandparents' village. Sofia felt cheated, as if something had been taken from her. On the metro home she scrolled through Layla's holiday photos and felt worse. Then she remembered that a year ago she had failed chemistry. And last summer in the village she had laughed more than in any summer before. Her B-plus hadn't changed. Only the person she was measuring against had.

qa.q: What grade did Layla get in chemistry?
qa.a: An A-minus.

qa.q: Why did Sofia feel cheated after Layla's grade?
qa.a: Comparing with Layla, who always seemed one step ahead, made her own best-ever grade feel as if something had been taken from her.

qa.q: What shift in comparison helped Sofia on the metro, and why?
qa.a: Comparing with herself a year ago, when she failed chemistry, which made her B-plus feel like the real progress it was.

qa.q: How might Layla see things, perhaps without knowing Sofia's feelings?
qa.a: Layla may simply be enjoying good grades and holidays, unaware of being the measuring stick for Sofia's mood.

grounding: A teenage girl with a decent situation feels cheated when she compares herself with a classmate one step ahead, and feels better when she compares with her own past.

passage: At the coaching institute, students were split into batches by test score. Ishita, sixteen, made it into Batch B, the second-highest of eight. Her parents were delighted; her cousin in Batch F would have given anything for it. But Ishita's desk looked straight across the corridor into Batch A's room, where Pranav and the others got the senior faculty and the air-conditioning. Every day she felt a sting, as if she'd been robbed. In the canteen she said, "It's so unfair. B gets nothing." Pranav, overhearing, laughed. "You should hear how A talks about last year's toppers." Ishita blinked. She thought of her cousin in Batch F, and of her own score a year ago. The sting didn't vanish, but it shrank.

qa.q: Which batch did Ishita make it into?
qa.a: Batch B, the second-highest of eight.

qa.q: Why did Ishita feel robbed despite being in Batch B?
qa.a: Her desk faced Batch A, so she kept comparing with those one step ahead and felt a sting of envy rather than pride in how well she had done.

qa.q: What helped Ishita's sting shrink, and why?
qa.a: Pranav's remark about Batch A comparing upward, and thinking of her cousin in Batch F and her own score a year ago, which changed whom she was looking at.

qa.q: What does Pranav's reply suggest about how Batch A feels?
qa.a: It suggests Batch A also compares upward and feels behind others, so feeling deprived depends on who you look at.

grounding: A teenage girl in the second-best batch feels cheated by facing the top batch every day, and the feeling shrinks when she looks at others and her own past.

passage:
Dear Irfan Bhai,

You asked why I sounded low on the phone. It's silly. Ammi and Abbu are fine, the shop is doing okay, and we got the roof fixed before the rains. But my friends' families all seem a step ahead. Rehan's dad bought a car, and Adil's family is moving to a bigger flat. When I'm with them I feel like we're struggling, and I come home angry at nothing. Then last week I helped Abbu with the month's accounts. We owe no one. We ate out on Eid. Our roof doesn't leak. If I compare us to five years ago, when we lived in one room, I should be grateful. I suppose it depends on who I'm looking at. Anyway, how is college? Write back.

Abhinav

qa.q: What did the family get fixed before the rains?
qa.a: The roof.

qa.q: How does Abhinav feel when with friends, and why?
qa.a: Abhinav feels the family is struggling and comes home angry, because the friends' families seem a step ahead.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Abhinav's view?
qa.a: Helping Abbu with the month's accounts and remembering living in one room five years ago, which showed the family is actually doing well.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel if he heard Abhinav say 'we're struggling'?
qa.a: Abbu might feel hurt or puzzled, since the shop is doing okay and the family owes no one.

grounding: A teenager whose family is doing decently feels deprived next to friends a step ahead, and sees in a letter that the feeling depends on whom they compare with.

passage: "Deepika, can I say something awful? I'm fifth in class. Fifth, out of forty-two. And I've been miserable for a week." Trisha pulled her knees up on the bench. "Because my whole group is one to four. Ananya's first, you're third. I'm the girl who's 'also in the group.' And it's not just marks. For the farewell party, everyone's getting new outfits stitched. Mine is Didi's old lehenga, which is actually lovely. But next to theirs it felt like a hand-me-down, which, okay, it is. Last night I cried and told Mummy it wasn't fair. She said, 'What isn't fair? You're fifth.' I couldn't explain. If I'd been in a group of kids ranked twentieth, I'd be the star. Same marks. Same lehenga. It's just who I'm standing next to. Isn't that stupid?"

qa.q: What rank is Trisha in her class?
qa.a: She is fifth out of forty-two.

qa.q: Why has Trisha been miserable for a week?
qa.a: She feels cheated and left behind because the friends she compares herself with are ranked one to four and have new farewell outfits.

qa.q: What could Trisha do with the insight she already reached?
qa.a: She could remind herself who she is measuring against, and look at how far she has come or at Didi's lovely lehenga for what it is, rather than next to her friends'.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel hearing Trisha say this?
qa.a: Deepika might be surprised, since fifth sounds excellent from where Deepika sits, and might feel a little awkward to be one of the people Trisha compares herself to.

grounding: A teenager with good marks and a decent outfit feels cheated because she compares herself only with friends a step ahead.

passage: I'm Tushar, Omkar's older brother, and I watched this happen at his under-sixteen cricket camp. Our parents had saved for months to buy him a proper willow bat for his birthday. He slept with it next to his pillow for two nights. Then he took it to camp. Three of the boys there, all a bit better than him, had full branded kits: helmets, pads, bags with their names stitched on. That evening Omkar put the bat in the corner and didn't oil it. When Papa asked about camp, he said, "It's fine," in a flat voice. At dinner he muttered, "Everyone else gets proper stuff." Papa looked at the bat in the corner and didn't say anything. I can't be sure what Omkar was thinking. But the bat hadn't changed. Only the boys next to him had.

qa.q: Where did Omkar sleep with his new bat for two nights?
qa.a: He slept with it next to his pillow.

qa.q: What does Omkar's flat 'It's fine' suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt let down and cheated after comparing his bat with the better kits of the boys a step ahead of him.

qa.q: What could Tushar do to help Omkar see his bat differently?
qa.a: Tushar could oil the bat with him and remind him how he felt on his birthday, before he started measuring it against the others' kits.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when he hears Omkar say everyone else gets proper stuff?
qa.a: Papa might feel hurt and quietly sad, since the family saved for months for a bat that now sits unoiled in the corner.

grounding: A teenager who got a good bat feels deprived after comparing himself with slightly better-equipped teammates, as seen by his brother.
